Issued at 230 AM MDT Fri Oct 30 2026

It is now October 30th. Where I grew up, in southern New England, 
this was know as Mischief Night. This was a night when young people 
did mostly harmless pranks, like shaving cream on a car or toilet 
paper one someones house or trees. We do have a couple of systems 
that will be moving through over the next few days, so it looks like 
the weather could cause some mischief as well.

We are dry right now. However, deeper moisture is noted over Nevada 
and Utah. And this moisture will ride northeastward, along with a 
shortwave that will start to bring some showers. However, today 
should be dry for most areas, especially East of the Divide. For 
most here, the day looks like a decent one with a mix of clouds and 
sun and above normal temperatures. There will be a bit of breeze at 
times as well in the wind prone areas from Rock Springs to Casper as 
flow will be southwest. Any showers today should be confined to 
western Wyoming, but even here chances are generally 1 out of 3 or 
less with most locations remaining dry. 

The deeper moisture from this wave should arrive tonight into 
Saturday and bring a better chance of showers. The main area of 
showers will be West of the Divide. Almost all locations East 
of the Divide have a 1 in 3 chance or less of a tenth of an inch
of rain from Friday night through the day on Saturday. The only
areas with a greater than 1 in 2 chance of a quarter of an inch
or more are the western mountains. And, with the southwest 
flow, this will be a warmer event. The 700 millibar temperatures
are expected to remain at 0 celsius or higher, with the warmest
temperatures further east. This would keep snow levels above 
8500 feet with any snow accumulation limited to above 10000 feet
in the western mountains. So, travel problems are not expected 
through this timeframe. And there is some good news for trick or
treating or holiday parties. It looks like most of the area 
will be in between systems for most of Saturday evening and even
late at night, so most areas should be rain free. There is a 
small chance of showers in far western Wyoming but the chance is
less than 1 out of 3 until after around 3 am.

The main show still looks to be from Sunday into Monday, and this is 
where some mischief in the weather would most likely be found. The 
players remain the same as yesterday, with a longwave trough and 
upper level low moving eastward and another low with a feed of 
Pacific moisture moving in from the southwest. All in all, reasoning 
looks the same as yesterday at this time. The systems are expected 
to phase. The heaviest precipitation should remain to the south of 
Wyoming. Most of the area, with the exception of portions of the Big 
Horn Basin, Wind River Basin and southern Green River Basin have at 
least a 1 in 2 chance of a quarter of an inch of precipitation or 
more. The greater than 1 in 2 chance of 0.75 inches of liquid is 
generally restricted to the mountains. In the lower elevations, the 
best chance would be in areas favored by northerly upslope flow, 
places like Casper, Lander and south of Worland. Buffalo may also 
see more, where there could be wrap around precipitation as the low 
moves to the east. Timing is coming more into focus as well. The 
steadiest precipitation in western Wyoming looks to be from midday 
Sunday through Sunday evening. East of the Divide, the steadiest 
would be Sunday night into Monday morning. All precipitation should 
end Monday night as the low moves into the Plains States.

The next question is, what about snow and how much? Somewhat cooler 
air will move into western Wyoming during the day on Sunday, but 
will really spread across the entire area Sunday night into Monday. 
At this time, the lower elevations look to be largely rain. The 
colder air in most locations doesn't get deep enough until most of 
the moisture is east of the area. Snow levels look to be around 6000 
feet by Monday morning. Places like Dubois may see some snow, and 
some lower elevations may see some flakes in the air Monday morning, 
but accumulation looks slim to none. The western valleys will likely 
see some snow, but again, accumulations at this time look like a 
coating at the most. The mountains obviously look more interesting. 
Most locations above 10000 feet have at least a 1 in 2 chance of 6 
inches of snow or more, but the chance of a foot or more is 
generally restricted to above 11500 feet. It could get slick over 
some of the higher passes though, especially Togwotee and Granite 
Passes, and possibly Powder River or Teton Passes. We may need some 
advisories for the higher elevations (greater than a 1 in 2 chance). 
However, since the main impacts are still more than 48 hours away, 
we will hold off for now.
